conditions_text: FOR THIN POLYMETHYLMETHACRYLATE AT 1 atm; Experiment: 30±5 mm/s
statement: For thin polymethylmethacrylate at 1 atm and 16 percent O2, the measured critical extinction velocity was 30±5 mm/s.

conditions_text: thin fuel in the thermal limit; opposed-flow flame spread
quantity: flame spread rate dependence on opposing-flow velocity
statement: For thin-fuel opposed-flow flame spread, the experimental results were independent of opposing-flow velocity in the identified thermal limit.
source_quote: A comparison between the two datasets allow us to establish the thermal limit for thin fuel for which the spread rate is independent of the opposing flow velocity.

conditions_text: opposed-flow flame spread data over varying thicknesses; ISS microgravity data and downward-spread normal-gravity data
quantity: fit of classical thin-fuel spread-rate formula
statement: For polymethylmethacrylate, the classical thin-fuel spread-rate formula fit the experimental results well when the adiabatic flame temperature was used in its flame coefficient.
source_quote: The classical thin fuel spread rate formula is shown to fit well with the experimental results provided the adiabatic flame temperature is used in the flame coefficient that appears in the formula.

conditions_text: In the thermal regime; if the O2 level is reduced
statement: In the thermal regime, reducing oxygen decreases the fuel consumption rate and increases the gas-phase combustion timescale; extinction occurs when that timescale becomes comparable to the gas residence time.
safety_implication: Lower oxygen can still lead to flame extinction, but the document does not provide a numerical oxygen limit for this condition.
source_quote: If the O2 level is reduced, the fuel consumption rate F′′′ decreases increasing tg,chem and finite-rate chemistry becomes important, leading to flame extinction, when tg,chem becomes comparable to tg,res.

conditions_text: If Vg is high enough
quantity: gas residence time at blowoff extinction
statement: In the thermal regime, a sufficiently high opposing-flow velocity shortens gas residence time until it is comparable to the combustion timescale, causing blowoff extinction.
source_quote: Even if there is sufficient O2, if Vg is high enough, tg,res can decrease to the point that it becomes comparable to tg,chem and finite-rate kinetics becomes important leading to blowoff extinction.

conditions_text: For thermally thin and thermally thick fuels, respectively, under the expressions in Equation (2.9).
quantity: flame spread rate dependence on opposing-flow velocity
statement: Under the reported spread-rate expressions, thermally thin fuels have a flame spread rate independent of opposing-flow velocity, whereas thermally thick fuels have a spread rate proportional to opposing-flow velocity.
source_quote: One of the remarkable aspects of these expressions is that the spread rate is independent of opposing flow velocity Vg for thin fuels while it is proportional to Vg for thick fuels.

conditions_text: Downward flame spread over a 50-µm-thick, 2-cm-wide PMMA sheet in forced opposed airflow.
quantity: flame spread rate dependence on forced opposing airflow
statement: For downward flame spread over 50-µm-thick, 2-cm-wide PMMA sheets, spread rate remained relatively independent of forced opposing airflow until the airflow reached 40 cm/s.
source_quote: To illustrate this, average spread rate data acquired in a vertical combustion tunnel (Ref. 18) for various opposing airflow velocity for spread over a thin sheet of PMMA (50-µm-thick, 2-cm-wide) is plotted in Figure 2.15. The spread rate can be seen to remain relatively independent of the forced opposing flow velocity until it reaches a value of 40 cm/s.

conditions_text: Downward flame spread; computational work used a one-step second-order global kinetics model.
statement: A cited computational study suggested that kinetic effects may be present during downward flame spread at 21 percent O2, but the report states that this conclusion cannot be established definitively from the computational results alone.
source_quote: The independence of spread rate with opposing flow velocity was interpreted as a constant kinetic effect by the buoyancy-generated flow. However, given the simplicity of the chemical kinetic model (one-step overall reaction) used in the computational model, a definitive conclusion cannot be made from computational results alone.

statement: In the BASS-II tests, the three Nomex samples did not ignite.
safety_implication: Nomex used as an ISS fire barrier did not ignite in these tests.
equipment_implication: Nomex is used aboard the ISS as a fire barrier.
source_quote: The three Nomex® samples did not ignite, which is an excellent result for fire safety aboard the ISS.

conditions_text: opposed flow; initial 3 cm/s; five different flow velocities
quantity: flow velocities at which the candle burned
statement: A wax candle ignited and burned in opposed flow at five flow velocities in the BASS-II test.
source_quote: The wax candle test successfully ignited in an opposed flow (akin to holding a candle upside down) and burned at five different flow velocities corresponding to the test matrix potentiometer settings as shown in Figure 3.1.

conditions_text: opposed flow; wick ejects droplet of wax directly upstream
statement: In microgravity opposed-flow tests, a burning candle wick ejected a wax droplet directly upstream, illustrating a possible ignition hazard from burning droplets ejected by low-viscosity melt.
safety_implication: Burning droplets from low-viscosity melting plastics may travel and ignite other materials in microgravity.
source_quote: The ejected wax droplet shown in Figure 3.1(b) typifies the flame spread hazard associated with melting plastics in microgravity. If the melt viscosity is low enough, burning droplets can be ejected and possibly ignite other materials.

material: black cast PMMA rods (0.00635 m and 0.009525 m diameter)
conditions_text: Sustained flame spread for the conditions tested; opposed-flow velocities below approximately 4 mm/s
quantity: opposed-flow velocity below which sustained flame spread was not observed
statement: For black cast PMMA rods of 0.00635 m and 0.009525 m diameter, sustained microgravity opposed-flame spread was not observed below approximately 4 mm/s opposed-flow velocity under the tested conditions.
safety_implication: Under the tested conditions, sustained flame spread was not observed below approximately 4 mm/s for these two rod diameters.
source_quote: Sustained flame spread for the conditions tested was not observed for opposed-flow velocities below approximately 4 mm/s for the 0.00635- and 0.009525-m-diameter rods.

conditions_text: average flame spread rate; opposed-flow velocity within the small range of flow velocities tested
statement: For black PMMA rods in microgravity, average opposed-flame spread rate increased with opposed-flow velocity over the tested range.
source_quote: As can be seen in Figure 4.1(a), the average flame spread rate increases with opposed-flow velocity, even within the small range of flow velocities tested.

conditions_text: opposed-flow flame spread; results particularly marked for 6.35-mm-diameter rods
statement: For black PMMA rods in microgravity, flame spread rate trended upward as oxygen concentration increased, particularly for the 6.35-mm-diameter rods.
source_quote: In Figure 4.1(b), the data exhibits an upward trend in spread rate with increasing O2 concentration, which is especially marked in the results of the 6.35-mm-diameter rods.

conditions_text: 1 mm thick; 2.2 cm wide; two sides burning; opposed flow; flow velocities 5, 3, and 2 cm/s
statement: For 1 mm thick, 2.2 cm wide PMMA burned on two sides in opposed flow, the measured flame spread rates were 0.144, 0.1309, and 0.1062 mm/s at flow velocities of 5, 3, and 2 cm/s, respectively.

conditions_text: 5 mm thick; 2.2 cm wide; two sides burning; opposed flow
statement: For 5 mm thick, 2.2 cm wide PMMA burned on two sides in opposed flow at 10 cm/s, the measured flame spread rate was 0.012 mm/s.

conditions_text: microgravity; model employs the same test sample and MSG geometry as the experiment
statement: The FDS model of flat PMMA samples in microgravity predicted a higher flame spread rate than the experiments observed.
source_quote: The model employs the same test sample and MSG geometry as the experiment. The model predicts a higher flame spread rate than that observed in experiments.

conditions_text: Below an initial O2 concentration of ~14.5 percent O2
statement: Clear cast PMMA cylindrical rods in microgravity could not achieve sustained ignition below an initial oxygen concentration of approximately 14.5 percent, despite flames being observed while the igniter was on and briefly after it was turned off.
safety_implication: The ignition limit depends on the ignition conditions and should not be treated as the oxygen concentration below which an already burning PMMA rod will necessarily extinguish.
source_quote: Below an initial O2 concentration of ~14.5 percent O2, a sustained ignition could not be achieved even though flames were observed when the igniter was on and briefly after the igniter was turned off before extinguishing.

conditions_text: Flames ignited at a higher O2 concentration and survived to final O2 concentrations as low as 13.6 percent O2
quantity: minimum final oxygen concentration sustaining a flame
statement: In microgravity, clear cast PMMA rods that ignited at higher oxygen concentrations sustained flames as the final ambient oxygen concentration fell to 13.6 percent O2.
safety_implication: A PMMA rod that cannot be ignited at a given oxygen level may still continue burning at a lower oxygen level after it has been ignited.
source_quote: Despite this limiting O2 concentration for ignition, flames ignited at a higher O2 survived to final O2 concentrations as low as 13.6 percent O2, indicating that the high heat loss to the initially cold rod will quench a postignition flame while a developed solid phase temperature profile allows a sustained flame down to these low ambient O2 concentrations.

conditions_text: Ignition generally occurred at a forced flow of 5 cm/s; below an initial O2 concentration of 16 percent, ignition delay increased significantly, with larger rods taking longer to ignite
statement: For clear cast PMMA rods in microgravity, ignition generally occurred within approximately 40 seconds at higher oxygen concentrations, but ignition delay increased significantly below 16 percent O2 and reached as long as 230 seconds for larger rods.
safety_implication: A short ignition exposure may fail to ignite PMMA even when a longer exposure could establish a sustained flame, particularly at lower oxygen concentrations and for larger rods.
equipment_implication: Ignition procedures with short exposure times may not reveal whether PMMA can sustain combustion after a longer ignition attempt.
source_quote: At higher O2 concentrations, ignition occurred within approximately 40 s. Below an initial O2 concentration of 16 percent, the ignition delay time increased significantly. Larger rods take longer to ignite, especially at lower O2 concentrations (up to 230 s).

conditions_text: NASA’s Test 1 is an upward flame spread test that has a fixed ignition time of ~25 s
statement: The report concludes that NASA Test 1's fixed ignition time of approximately 25 seconds may be too short for a flammability test and may instead function as an ignition test.
safety_implication: Passing NASA Test 1 after its fixed ignition period may not establish that a material cannot ignite under a longer exposure.
equipment_implication: The report warns that the fixed ignition time may make NASA Test 1 an ignition test rather than a sufficient flammability test.
source_quote: NASA Test 1 25-s ignition time may be too short for flammability test and so may be an ignition test.

material: clear cast PMMA cylindrical rod (r = 0.476 cm)
conditions_text: The initial O2 setting was 14.8 percent O2 (by volume) and the final O2 reading was 13.6 percent O2; flow changed from 2 to 1.5 cm/s
statement: During a microgravity quenching test of a clear cast PMMA rod with radius 0.476 cm, at a final oxygen concentration of 13.6 percent, the rod reached an apparently steady-state regression rate of 0.0385 mm/s after the flow changed from 2 to 1.5 cm/s.
source_quote: The flow was incrementally decreased throughout the test, as shown by the red stepped line. The flame length stopped growing at the 2- to 1.5-cm/s flow change, and shortly thereafter the rod regression reached an apparently steady-state regression rate of 0.0385 mm/s.

conditions_text: as the initial O2 concentration decreases; low ambient O2 levels in microgravity
statement: For PMMA burning in microgravity at low ambient O2 concentrations, the CO-to-CO2 ratio increased as initial O2 decreased and was an order of magnitude greater than the 1g cone-calorimeter values, indicating less efficient burning.
safety_implication: Higher CO production relative to CO2 under low-O2 microgravity conditions may increase crew exposure to carbon monoxide.
source_quote: The CO to CO2 ratio is plotted against the initial O2 concentration in Figure 6.15, and shows that as the initial O2 concentration decreases, the CO to CO2 ratio increases. These values are an order of magnitude greater than the 1g values found in the cone calorimeter for PMMA (Ref. 24), indicating very inefficient burning at low ambient O2 levels in microgravity.

conditions_text: At higher O2 concentrations; at lower O2 concentrations
statement: For PMMA burning in microgravity, flames were nearly stoichiometric at higher O2 concentrations, while the global equivalence ratio increased at lower O2 concentrations, indicating that O2 rather than fuel was the limiting reactant.
source_quote: At higher O2 concentrations, the flames are nearly stoichiometric. At lower O2 concentrations, the global equivalence ratio increases. This indicates that the limiting reactant is the O2 rather than the fuel.

conditions_text: along the flammability boundary; for quenching extinction (a < ~10 s–1)
statement: In the analyzed flammability-boundary model, the predicted critical flame temperature for the fuel decreases as stretch rate a decreases, with a more rapid drop for quenching extinction at a < ~10 s–1.
source_quote: The resultant critical flame temperature along the flammability boundary is shown in Figure 6.17 as a function of a. The critical temperature drops as a decreases. For quenching extinction (a < ~10 s–1), the critical flame temperature drops more precipitously.

conditions_text: along the flammability boundary; stagnation region of the rod
quantity: convective heating rate dependence on stretch rate
statement: The analysis predicts that convective heating rate to the PMMA rod's stagnation region depends linearly on stretch rate a along the flammability boundary.
source_quote: The convective heating rate is linear with a, as shown in Figure 6.17. This is an interesting combination of a terms in Equation (6.4): the square root Nu flow dependence (Eq. (6.3)), the approximate minus cube root s dependence (0.334 power from Figure 6.12), and the approximate seventh root temperature difference (Tcrit – Ts) dependence on a (0.16 power from Figure 6.17).

conditions_text: The minimum in the flammability boundary is at a of 8 to 12 s–1, where the a is modified to account for the various rod sizes tested through the gas-phase ℓ scale.
statement: For clear and black PMMA rods tested in microgravity, the minimum of the flammability boundary occurred at a stretch rate of 8 to 12 s–1, with the stretch rate modified for the different rod sizes using the gas-phase length scale.
safety_implication: This boundary identifies conditions near the lowest oxygen flammability limit that should be considered when assessing PMMA fire risk in microgravity.
source_quote: The minimum in the flammability boundary is at a of 8 to 12 s–1, where the a is modified to account for the various rod sizes tested through the gas-phase ℓ scale.

conditions_text: as the minimum limiting O2 concentration is approached
statement: In the BASS-II microgravity tests, ignition delay for the tested rods increased as the minimum limiting oxygen concentration was approached, and could reach almost 10 times the NASA STD–6001 standard igniter on time.
safety_implication: An ignition test duration based on the standard igniter on time may not capture the longer ignition delays observed near the limiting oxygen concentration.
equipment_implication: The NASA STD–6001 igniter on time is a comparison benchmark; observed delays could be almost 10 times longer.
source_quote: Ignition delay time increased significantly as the minimum limiting O2 concentration is approached. Ignition limits are found to be at higher O2 concentrations than the flammability limits due to the added heat loss to the initially cold fuel rod present at ignition. The ignition delay time can be up to almost 10 times longer than the NASA STD–6001 standard igniter on time.

conditions_text: the added heat loss to the initially cold fuel rod present at ignition
quantity: oxygen concentration at ignition limit relative to flammability limit
statement: In the BASS-II microgravity tests, ignition limits for the tested rods occurred at higher oxygen concentrations than their flammability limits because the initially cold rod added heat loss during ignition.
safety_implication: Flammability limits alone do not represent the higher oxygen concentrations needed to ignite the initially cold rods under these test conditions.
source_quote: Ignition limits are found to be at higher O2 concentrations than the flammability limits due to the added heat loss to the initially cold fuel rod present at ignition.

conditions_text: As flow speed is increased
statement: In the BASS-II microgravity tests, increasing flow speed initiated blowoff by forming a hole in the flame sheet at the PMMA rod stagnation region; after the stagnation region was displaced downstream by more than one gas-phase thermal length ℓ, the flame could not propagate upstream again even when flow was reduced.
safety_implication: Once blowoff progresses beyond the stated thermal-length threshold, reducing flow may not restore the flame, which is relevant to interpreting fire behavior during ventilation changes.
equipment_implication: The reported blowoff behavior depends on flow speed and stagnation-region displacement.
source_quote: As flow speed is increased, blowoff extinction is initiated by the formation of a hole in the flame sheet in the stagnation region of the flame. Once the stagnation region is blown far enough downstream of the stagnation region (greater than one gas-phase thermal length ℓ), the flame is unable to propagate back upstream even when the flow is reduced.

conditions_text: ISS experiments and Zero Gravity Research Facility 5.18-s drop test limits
statement: The BASS-II ISS experiment's PMMA rod blowoff extinction limits agreed well with limits from Zero Gravity Research Facility 5.18-s drop tests.
source_quote: Blowoff extinction limits from the ISS experiments agree well with Zero Gravity Research Facility 5.18-s drop test limits.

conditions_text: as the minimum O2 concentration is approached
quantity: global equivalence behavior, CO production, and CO to CO2 ratio
statement: For PMMA rod flames near the minimum oxygen concentration in microgravity, gas sensor data and rod mass-loss estimates indicated increasingly fuel-rich global flames, with excess pyrolyzate escaping from the open flame tail; CO production and the CO to CO2 ratio also increased as oxygen concentration fell.
safety_implication: Near the minimum oxygen concentration, these flames produced more CO and leaked unburned pyrolyzate, indicating combustion products and incomplete combustion warrant attention in fire-risk assessment.
source_quote: Gas sensor data and rod mass loss estimates indicate that the flames are globally stoichiometric at higher O2 concentrations but become more globally fuel rich as the minimum O2 concentration is approached. This is due to excess pyrolyzate leakage out of the open tail of the hemispherical flames. CO production also increases significantly at low O2 levels.

conditions_text: On the quenching branch of Figure 6.22, as the U is reduced
quantity: ambient O2 concentration at the quenching limit
statement: For PMMA rods near the quenching branch in microgravity, reducing flow required higher ambient oxygen concentration at the flammability limit to provide an adequate oxygen gradient for diffusion to the flame.
safety_implication: The minimum oxygen condition for flame persistence depends on flow; lower flow near quenching was associated with a higher required ambient oxygen concentration.
source_quote: On the quenching branch of Figure 6.22, as the U is reduced, the ambient O2 concentration at the limit has to increase to create an adequate O2 gradient for diffusion of O2 to the flame.

conditions_text: for this geometry; U/UD = 1
quantity: transition from blowoff to quenching relative to diffusive velocity
statement: For the tested PMMA rod geometry, the transition from blowoff to quenching occurred when forced-flow velocity became the same order as the diffusive velocity, with the reported diffusive velocity UD equal to 2 cm/s.
equipment_implication: The reported transition is associated with forced-flow velocity becoming comparable to diffusive velocity.
source_quote: The transition from blowoff to quenching occurs when the forced-flow velocity becomes the same order as the diffusive velocity (U/UD = 1) for this geometry.

conditions_text: at low a
quantity: effect of gas-phase radiative feedback on flammability
statement: For the tested PMMA rods, gas-phase radiative feedback became an important heat-transfer process at low stretch rates and extended flammability to lower a.
safety_implication: Radiative feedback can sustain PMMA flammability at lower stretch rates than would occur without that heat-transfer contribution.
source_quote: Gas-phase radiative feedback becomes an important heat transfer process that extends the flammability limit to lower a.

material: SIBAL fabric (75 percent cotton and 25 percent fiberglass)
conditions_text: low-speed concurrent forced flows; Ambient O2 was varied from 21 percent down to 16 percent
statement: In microgravity, a 75 percent cotton and 25 percent fiberglass SIBAL fabric sample burning in concurrent forced flow quenched at flow speeds between 1 and 5 cm/s, with the quenching speed higher at lower oxygen concentrations of 16 to 21 percent.
safety_implication: The reported quenching range identifies low-flow conditions where this fabric's flame may extinguish, but the higher quenching speed at lower oxygen shows that the limit depends on oxygen concentration.
source_quote: The quenching speeds were found to be between 1 and 5 cm/s with higher speed in lower O2 atmosphere.

conditions_text: Steady flame spread rates in different flow speeds and O2 percentages; both 2.2- and 1.2-cm samples
statement: In microgravity, SIBAL fabric flames spread more slowly on narrower samples, at lower flow velocities, and at lower oxygen percentages.
source_quote: Flames spread more slowly across the narrower samples, at lower flow velocities and at lower O2 percentages.

conditions_text: 2.2-cm sample; 10-cm/s flow; 21 percent O2
quantity: time to steady spread; steady spread duration; total combustion time
statement: A 2.2-cm-wide SIBAL fabric sample in 21 percent oxygen and 10 cm/s flow reached a steady spread state at about 19 s, maintained it for around 9 s, and completed combustion in about 40 s.
source_quote: At about 19 s, the flame reached a limiting constant length and a steady spread rate relative to the laboratory (Ref. 11). This steady spread state lasted for around 9 s. ... The whole combustion process took about 40 s.

conditions_text: 2.2-cm sample; 5-cm/s flow; 21 percent O2
quantity: total burn time; steady spread duration
statement: A 2.2-cm-wide SIBAL fabric sample in 21 percent oxygen and 5 cm/s flow took more than 60 s to burn completely and had a steady spread period of about 21 s.
source_quote: Because the flow speed is lower, it took more than 60 s to burn the whole sample. Steady spread time lasts for about 21 s, much longer than the 10-cm/s flow case.

conditions_text: low-speed purely forced flows
statement: In microgravity low-speed purely forced flows, thin flat cotton-fiberglass composite fabric flames had quenching extinction velocities between 1 and 5 cm/s.
safety_implication: Microgravity fire assessments should account for flame persistence and extinction behavior at forced-flow velocities between 1 and 5 cm/s.
source_quote: The quenching velocities are small (between 1 and 5 cm/s), and an accurate determination is necessary to resolve the slope of the quenching boundary.

conditions_text: low flow velocities; radiative and conductive losses
statement: Microgravity experiments with thin flat cotton-fiberglass composite fabric qualitatively supported theoretical predictions that radiative and conductive losses produce solid-fuel flammability limits at low flow velocities.
source_quote: The experimental data obtained supports earlier theoretical predictions (at least qualitatively) of solid flammability limits at low flow velocities due to radiative and conductive losses.

conditions_text: at quenching
statement: In microgravity, a quenching thin flat cotton-fiberglass composite fabric flame shrank in both length and width before extinguishing in a three-dimensional manner.
safety_implication: Flame monitoring and extinction assessments in microgravity should account for three-dimensional flame contraction during quenching.
source_quote: The flame image sequence at quenching shows the flame shrinks both in length and width and the flame goes out in a three-dimensional manner.

conditions_text: Ignited briefly but did not spread at all and extinguished while the igniter was still on
statement: The Nomex® sample did not sustain flame spread in the reported test, briefly igniting before extinguishing while the igniter was still on.
source_quote: Ignited briefly but did not spread at all and extinguished while the igniter was still on

conditions_text: Tried to ignite, flame would not sustain
statement: The Nomex® sample did not sustain a flame when ignition was attempted in the reported test.
source_quote: Tried to ignite, flame would not sustain

conditions_text: Opposed; very slow increments; finite low flow
statement: The 6.35-mm black rod had a very slow flame that extinguished at flow restrictor potentiometer setting 0.315 during an opposed-flow test.
source_quote: Broke –20, –21 igniters, –22 worked; nice flame, got down to extinction at pot 0.315 (finite low flow), very slow increments

conditions_text: Opposed; steady burn at multiple velocities; finite quench at pot 0.3
statement: The 6.35-mm black rod sustained steady burning at multiple velocities and quenched at flow restrictor potentiometer setting 0.3.
source_quote: HCl 0.3 > 0.9, steady burn at multiple velocities, finite quench at pot 0.3

conditions_text: Opposed; oscillating at 0.36, out immediately at 0.34; multiple steady spread flows
statement: The 9.525-mm black rod showed oscillation at potentiometer setting 0.36 and extinguished immediately at 0.34 during an opposed-flow test.
source_quote: Loss of signal before extinguished, oscillating at 0.36, out immediately at 0.34, multiple steady spread flows

conditions_text: Opposed; fan pot 1.1 (5 cm/s); flame reached front of sample and began to wrap around
statement: The 12.7-mm black rod flame reached the front of the sample and began to wrap around during the reported opposed-flow test.
source_quote: Fan pot 1.1 (5 cm/s), 0.4, 0.36, 0.32, 0.3, 0.28, 0.26; flame out when pot turned to 0; HCL 0.5 > 4.1; flame reached front of sample and began to wrap around

conditions_text: Opposed; fan pot 1.3 (5cm/s), 0.4, 0.36, 0.32
statement: The 12.7-mm black rod flame extinguished when the fan potentiometer was set to 0.32 in the reported opposed-flow test.
source_quote: Fan pot 1.3 (5cm/s), 0.4, 0.36, 0.32; flame out when pot turned to 0.32

conditions_text: Opposed; all blue; extinguished at 0.31
statement: The 6.35-mm black rod extinguished at potentiometer setting 0.31 in the reported opposed-flow test.
source_quote: All blue, extinguished at 0.31

conditions_text: Opposed; fan setting (0.36)
statement: The 6.35-mm black rod sustained a stable burn with a sooty tail and blue leading edge during the reported opposed-flow test.
source_quote: Nice stable burn with sooty tail but blue leading edge

conditions_text: Concurrent; extinguished at pot 0.32
statement: The 6.35-mm black rod extinguished at potentiometer setting 0.32 during the reported concurrent-flow test.
source_quote: Extinguished at pot 0.32, one high flow setting

conditions_text: Opposed; tried blowoff without success; returned to 2 cm/s; oscillated and extinguished at 0.34
statement: The 6.35-mm rod extinguished at potentiometer setting 0.34 after oscillating, and its leading edge receded slightly without blowing off.
source_quote: A few finite flows, then tried blowoff without success, turned back down to 2 cm/s, then 0.36, 0.34 pots, oscillated and out at 0.34; leading edge receded slightly but did not blowoff

conditions_text: Opposed; alternated fan pot between 1 and 2 at 1-min intervals, then reduced slowly
statement: The 6.35-mm black rod extinguished at fan potentiometer setting 0.32 during the reported opposed-flow test.
source_quote: Alternated fan pot between 1 and 2 at 1-min intervals to try to get time constant resolution; finally turned pot down slowly, extinction at fan pot 0.32

conditions_text: Concurrent; tried blowoff at pot 10 with 2 restrictors; flame out at 0.32
statement: The 6.35-mm black rod did not blow off at fan potentiometer setting 10 with 2 restrictors and extinguished at 0.32.
source_quote: Tried blowoff, did not blowoff at pot 10 2 restrictors, flame out at 0.32, sample mostly gone

conditions_text: Opposed; stable flame at pot 0.33; fan off, not slow ramp
statement: The 6.35-mm black rod had a stable flame at potentiometer setting 0.33, but extinction was not established because the fan was switched off rather than slowly ramped down.
source_quote: Nice stable burn at low velocity, mostly blue with some inner soot at higher flow, stable flame at pot 0.33, did not get extinction on stills, but was just fan off, not slow ramp

conditions_text: Opposed; alternated fan pot between 1 and 2 at 1-min intervals, then turned pot down slowly
statement: The 6.35-mm black rod extinguished at fan potentiometer setting 0.335 during the reported opposed-flow test.
source_quote: Alternated fan pot between 1 and 2 at 1-min intervals to try to get time constant resolution; finally turned pot down slowly, extinction at fan pot 0.335

conditions_text: Opposed; after sample end became flat; dim flame
statement: The 6.35-mm black rod self-extinguished at 5 cm/s after the sample end became flat, producing a dim flame.
source_quote: Flame self-extinguished at 5 cm/s after sample end became flat, dim flame

material: PMMA slab, 4 mm thick and 1 cm wide
conditions_text: flame self-extinguished at 8 cm/s after almost 10 min
statement: A 4-mm-thick, 1-cm-wide PMMA slab in microgravity self-extinguished at an airflow of 8 cm/s after almost 10 minutes of burning.
safety_implication: A PMMA flame may persist for minutes in microgravity before extinguishing at reduced airflow, so it should not be assumed to go out quickly.
source_quote: flame self-extinguished at 8 cm/s after almost 10 min;

material: PMMA, 1 cm wide and 5 mm thick
conditions_text: 29-min burn; extinguished at 12 cm/s
statement: A 5-mm-thick, 1-cm-wide PMMA sample in microgravity burned for 29 minutes and extinguished at an airflow of 12 cm/s.
safety_implication: A PMMA fire can burn for an extended period in microgravity and extinguish only under a specific airflow condition.
source_quote: 29-min burn; extinguished at 12 cm/s., HCl 0.5 > 5.0

material: PMMA, 2 mm thick, one-sided, 2 cm wide
conditions_text: flame self-extinguished at an air reading of 9 cm/s
statement: A 2-mm-thick, 2-cm-wide, one-sided PMMA sample in microgravity self-extinguished at an air reading of 9 cm/s.
safety_implication: A PMMA flame in microgravity may self-extinguish at a nonzero airflow, but this result is specific to the tested sample and conditions.
source_quote: Prolonged ignition, followed by flow reduction after flame moved away from igniter region and spread steadily; flame self-extinguished at an air reading of 9 cm/s.

material: PMMA, 2 cm wide and 3 mm thick
conditions_text: 26-min burn; flow briefly at 15 cm/s but flame was too strong so turned down; extinguished 8 cm/s
statement: A 2-cm-wide, 3-mm-thick PMMA sample in microgravity burned for 26 minutes and extinguished at an airflow of 8 cm/s.
safety_implication: A PMMA flame can persist for many minutes in microgravity, and the tested flame was reported as too strong at 15 cm/s.
source_quote: 26-min burn; flow briefly at 15 cm/s but flame was too strong so turned down; HCl 0 > 3.1,  extinguished 8 cm/s

material: PMMA, 1 mm thick and 2 cm wide
conditions_text: Burned at decreasing flow down to 1 cm/s or so, still fine; at end of sample, turned up flow to 10 cm/s and flame got really long
statement: A 1-mm-thick, 2-cm-wide PMMA sample in microgravity continued burning as airflow was decreased to about 1 cm/s; increasing airflow to 10 cm/s made the flame really long, and soot was reported on the door and heat sink.
safety_implication: PMMA burning persisted at very low airflow in this test, while a later increase in airflow was associated with a much longer flame and soot deposition.
source_quote: Burned at decreasing flow down to 1 cm/s or so, still fine, at end of sample, turned up flow to 10 cm/s and flame got really long; Alex reported some soot on the door and some on the heat sink;

conditions_text: 4-mm-thick, 2-cm, two-sided PMMA slab; opposed flow; calibrated initial O2 19.0 vol%, calibrated final O2 17.4 vol%.
statement: A 4-mm-thick, two-sided PMMA slab in an opposed-flow test continued burning as flow decreased and extinguished on its own at 5 cm/s.
safety_implication: The tested slab sustained burning as flow was reduced until it extinguished at 5 cm/s.
source_quote: Burned with decreasing flows until it went out on its own at 5 cm/s

conditions_text: 3-mm-thick PMMA one-sided, 2 cm wide; opposed flow; calibrated initial O2 22.2 vol%, calibrated final O2 21.2 vol%.
statement: A 3-mm-thick, one-sided PMMA sample ignited at 20 cm/s, but its flame self-extinguished after the flow was reduced and raised from 13 to 14 cm/s.
safety_implication: In this test, PMMA that ignited at 20 cm/s did not sustain its flame after flow was reduced to 13 cm/s and then increased to 14 cm/s.
source_quote: Ignite at 20 cm/s, turn down to 15 cm/s after spread away from igniter; seemed steady, so turned down to 13 cm/s; flame got very dim, so increased flow to 14 cm/s, but it self-extinguished

conditions_text: 5-mm-thick PMMA, 2 cm wide; opposed flow; calibrated initial O2 18.0 vol%, calibrated final O2 17.4 vol%.
statement: A 5-mm-thick, 2-cm-wide PMMA sample initially burned at 10 cm/s, then its flame went out after flow was reduced to 8 cm/s.
safety_implication: The observed flame extinguished after flow was lowered from the 10 cm/s ignition condition to 8 cm/s.
source_quote: ignition at 10 cm/s (left 8 min) then flow down to 8 cm/s (flame out after 3 more minutes)

conditions_text: 2-cm-wide, 5-mm-thick, one-sided PMMA; opposed flow; calibrated initial O2 20.8 vol%, calibrated final O2 19.7 vol%.
statement: A 2-cm-wide, 5-mm-thick, one-sided PMMA sample was reported extinguished at 18 cm/s.
safety_implication: The table records extinction at 18 cm/s for this specific PMMA sample and test.
source_quote: Extinguished at 18 cm/s; HCl 0.6 > 2.6

conditions_text: 12.7-mm clear PMMA rod; concurrent flow; calibrated initial O2 15.9 vol%, calibrated final O2 14.6 vol%; self-extinction at pot 0.31.
statement: A 12.7-mm clear PMMA rod in concurrent flow ignited and burned at five potentiometer settings, then self-extinguished after more than 3 minutes at pot 0.31.
safety_implication: The rod sustained burning across multiple tested settings but self-extinguished at the reported low-flow potentiometer setting.
source_quote: Ignited and burned at 5 pot settings, flame self-extinguished after 3+ min at pot 0.31

conditions_text: 9.525-mm clear rod; stagnation flow; first test calibrated initial O2 17.1 vol%, calibrated final O2 16.7 vol%; reburn of same rod calibrated initial O2 16.7 vol%, calibrated final O2 15.6 vol%.
statement: A 9.525-mm clear PMMA rod in stagnation flow self-extinguished at pot 0.32 in one test, while a reburn of the same rod self-extinguished at the lower pot setting of 0.27.
safety_implication: The reburn extinguished at a lower potentiometer setting than the preceding test of the same rod, so the extinction condition was not repeatable across these runs.
source_quote: Decrease flow to extinction at 0.32 pot, from 0.35 pot.

conditions_text: Concurrent flow; 6.35-mm clear rod; flame sooty at 5 cm/s
statement: A 6.35-mm clear PMMA rod flame in concurrent flow extinguished when the flow was turned down; the flame was sooty at 5 cm/s.
source_quote: Flame extinguished as soon as he turned flow down, probably overshot, flame sooty at 5 cm/s

conditions_text: 9.525-mm clear rod; stagnation flow; stepped through 5, 0.7, 0.5, 0.4, 0.36 to extinction
statement: A 9.525-mm clear PMMA rod in stagnation flow extinguished at a flow setting of 0.36 as the flow was reduced.
source_quote: Larger rod, decreased flow, extinguished at 0.36, HCl 9.7

conditions_text: 2 cm SIBAL; flame spread across the whole sample at 3 cm/s
statement: A 2 cm SIBAL sample flame spread across the whole sample at 3 cm/s.
source_quote: Initial HCl 0.2 final 0.5, no HCN, flame spread whole sample at 3 cm/s

conditions_text: 2 cm SIBAL; extinguished as flow was reduced below 3 cm/s
statement: A 2 cm SIBAL sample flame extinguished when flow was reduced below 3 cm/s.
source_quote: Extinguished as we reduced flow below 3 cm/s

conditions_text: 1 cm SIBAL; air turned down to 3 cm/s
statement: A 1 cm SIBAL sample flame quickly extinguished when the air was turned down to 3 cm/s.
source_quote: Quick extinction when we turned air down to 3 cm/s, HCl 0.8 end

conditions_text: 1 cm SIBAL; ignited at 11, then flow turned down to 5
statement: A 1 cm SIBAL sample ignited at 11 and extinguished after the flow was turned down to 5.
source_quote: Ignited at 11, turned down to 5 and extinguished, HCl 2.0

conditions_text: 1 cm SIBAL; air display 11, maximum (47)
statement: A 1 cm SIBAL sample flame was successfully blown off at the maximum air display, shown as 47 cm/s.
source_quote: Successful blowoff! HCl still 0.8 end

conditions_text: MSG working volume V = 0.25 m3; gaseous N2 flow r = 0.0005 m3/min maximum; Cin = 0 (pure N2)
quantity: O2 concentration in the work volume as a function of time
statement: For pure-nitrogen dilution of the 0.25 m3 MSG work volume, the CSTR model predicts that oxygen concentration decreases exponentially with time according to c(t) = Co·exp(−(r/V)t).
equipment_implication: The model calculates how nitrogen flow changes the glovebox work-volume O2 concentration over time.
source_quote: The rate of change of the O2 concentration c(t) with time t within the work volume V equation is given by the flow of gaseous N2 (r) multiplied by the difference between the inlet (Cin) and outlet O2 concentrations (Cout)

conditions_text: On-orbit MSG nitrogen dilution; calibration and subsequent BASS-II operations across a range of dilution rates
quantity: Agreement between CSTR model predictions and CSA-CP O2 readings
statement: During on-orbit MSG nitrogen-dilution calibration and subsequent BASS-II operations, CSTR model predictions agreed very well with CSA-CP oxygen readings, including postdilution readings across a range of dilution rates.
equipment_implication: The model was used to determine nitrogen flow rate and dilution time for target test O2 concentrations.
source_quote: The model agrees very well with CSA-CP readings directly and corrected for the offset to provide a calibrated O2 level with time. This model was used for subsequent BASS–II operations to determine the N2 flow rate and flow time to achieve the desired test O2 concentration based upon the initial O2 concentration and operational crew time constraints. It worked very well, and postdilution CSA-CP readings agreed extremely well with the model predictions over a range of dilution rates, as shown in Figure B.2.

conditions_text: 2 cm SIBAL; flow settings listed as 5, 2, 1, <1; observation recorded HCL 0.9 at the end
statement: During BASS-II test T6, a 2 cm SIBAL sample still did not extinguish when the observation recorded HCL 0.9 at the end of the test.
source_quote: HCL 0.9 at the end, still did not extinguish

conditions_text: BASS–II microgravity flames
statement: BASS-II microgravity flames had CO-to-CO2 ratios well above the less-than-0.004 ratio typical of efficiently burned flue gases, indicating comparatively inefficient combustion.
safety_implication: Inefficient combustion can produce elevated CO, so fire safety assessment should account for toxic combustion products as well as flame behavior.
source_quote: For efficiently burned flue gases (boilers, furnaces, etc.), this ratio is typically less than 0.004. As can be seen, most of our data is well above that, indicating that microgravity flames are comparatively inefficient.

conditions_text: a fire of the scale of a BASS–II test diluted within the U.S. Lab (106-m3 pressurized volume)
statement: The estimated CO concentration from a BASS-II-scale fire diluted within the U.S. Lab would be 1.5 ppm, below the stated long-term 10 ppm and 1 hour 55 ppm SMAC values.
safety_implication: The estimate indicates this fire scale would remain below the cited CO exposure limits after dilution in the U.S. Lab, but does not establish concentrations near the fire or in other volumes.
source_quote: Since the ISS is quite large, the combustion products from a fire of the scale of a BASS–II test would quickly be diluted, so that even within just the U.S. Lab (106-m3 pressurized volume), the CO levels in the lab would only be 1.5 ppm, well below spacecraft maximum allowable concentration (SMAC) values for even long-term exposure (10 ppm), let alone the 1 hour SMAC of 55 ppm (Ref. 12).

conditions_text: small microgravity fires; duct flows varied between and within tests
statement: Estimated heat release rates for the tested small microgravity fires were typically well below 100 W, increased with ambient O2 concentration, and varied with duct flow.
safety_implication: The reported rates characterize these small tests only; the observed dependence on oxygen and flow means fire heat release should not be assumed constant across ventilation conditions.
equipment_implication: Duct flow affected the scatter in estimated heat release rates.
source_quote: Using his constant of 13.1 kJ/g O2, we estimate the HRRs to be typically well below 100 W, as shown in Figure 1.6. There is a trend of increasing HRR with increasing ambient O2 concentration, and the scatter is attributed to the different duct flows between and even within the tests.

conditions_text: one long opposed thick slab test; one relatively brief concurrent rod test
quantity: heat release rate and observed window damage
statement: A long opposed thick slab test released close to 100 W and damaged the lower downstream corner of the front window, while a relatively brief concurrent rod test releasing almost 110 W caused no damage.
safety_implication: The contrast indicates that exposure duration and heat direction or location can matter to hardware damage, not just peak heat release.
equipment_implication: The prolonged slab burn damaged the lower downstream corner of the front window; the brief rod burn did not cause damage.
source_quote: The one long opposed thick slab test that caused the lower downstream corner of the front window damage released close to 100 W. A prior relatively brief concurrent rod test that released almost 110 W did not cause any damage.

conditions_text: remaining 19 samples used for global equivalence ratio estimates
statement: In the usable BASS-II samples, CO generation generally increased with fuel mass loss and O2 consumption; the test with 7-g fuel mass loss exceeded 1,000 ppm CO, above the sensor range.
safety_implication: CO can exceed the measurement range during substantial fuel consumption, so monitoring systems need adequate range to characterize high-CO events.
equipment_implication: The CO sensor was exceeded in the 7-g fuel mass loss test.
source_quote: The CO data is more scattered, but CO generation generally increases with increasing fuel mass loss and O2 consumption. The 7-g fuel mass loss test had over 1,000 ppm of CO (above the range of the sensor).

conditions_text: low-velocity forced-flow conditions; effective equivalence ratio estimated using the observed slope of 0.4582 O2 vol% per gram of fuel and PMMA molecular weight of 100 g/gmol
statement: BASS-II tests had an estimated average global equivalence ratio of 1.3, indicating fuel-rich burning under low-velocity forced-flow conditions.
safety_implication: Fuel-rich burning under these tested conditions left some vaporized fuel incompletely burned, contributing to soot, CO, and unburned hydrocarbons.
equipment_implication: The reported low-velocity forced flow was associated with fuel-rich burning.
source_quote: Using the observed slope of 0.4582 O2 vol% per gram of fuel, and the molecular weight for PMMA of 100 g/gmol for the majority of the data, we can use the above equations to solve for the effective equivalence ratio for the tests: Φglobal = 1.3, which is fuel rich. So, in general, the flames were under-ventilated and did not burn all of the vaporized fuel.

conditions_text: tests with different geometries, flow velocities, and initial O2 concentrations
statement: BASS-II sensor data showed nearly stoichiometric conversion of O2 to CO2, while CO levels depended on geometry and in some cases the flow-velocity and geometry combination.
safety_implication: Combustion-product yields vary with fuel geometry and ventilation conditions, so CO production should not be inferred from oxygen consumption alone.
equipment_implication: Flow velocity combined with geometry affected CO levels in some tests.
source_quote: Sensor data from the tests showed that the O2 was burning nearly stoichiometrically to CO2, and that CO levels appear to be a function of geometry and, in some cases, the flow velocity and geometry combination.

conditions_text: ambient conditions of 21/79 (percent by volume) mixture of O2 and N2 at 1 atm pressure
statement: In the authors’ computations for thin polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) at 21 percent O2 and 1 atm, the extinction velocity was 1.5 cm/s for each of the four fuel thicknesses studied.
safety_implication: The consistent modeled threshold across thicknesses suggests airflow-based extinction criteria may apply across these thin PMMA fuel thicknesses under the stated conditions.
source_quote: Moreover, the extinction velocity is identical at 1.5 cm/s for all the four thicknesses studied.

conditions_text: 100-µm-thick sheet of PMMA; 16 percent O2; comparison at 21 percent O2
statement: For a 100-µm-thick PMMA sheet at 16 percent O2, the computational extinction velocity was 3.5 cm/s, compared with 1.5 cm/s at 21 percent O2.
safety_implication: Lower oxygen concentration does not necessarily make low-flow extinction easier for this modeled configuration; suppression design should account for the higher extinction velocity reported at reduced oxygen.
source_quote: The extinction velocity is found to be 3.5 cm/s as opposed to 1.5 cm/s at 21 percent O2.

conditions_text: downward spread configuration in a quiescent 1g environment; 21 percent O2
statement: In the model for downward flame spread over PMMA in quiescent normal gravity at 21 percent O2, steady spread rates were 2.8, 1.6, 1.2, and 0.9 mm/s for thicknesses of 100, 200, 300, and 400 µm, respectively.
source_quote: It should be mentioned that when the computational model is used (Ref. 15) for downward spread configuration in a quiescent 1g environment, a steady spread results for 21 percent O2 with spread rates of 2.8, 1.6, 1.2, and 0.9 mm/s, for 100, 200, 300 and 400 µm, respectively, as shown in Figure 2.11.

conditions_text: downward spread configuration in a quiescent 1g environment; 16 percent O2
statement: In the model for downward PMMA flame spread in quiescent normal gravity, the buoyancy-created flow at 16 percent O2 was strong enough to cause blowoff extinction.
source_quote: At 16 percent O2, however, the buoyancy-created flow is strong enough to cause blowoff extinction.

conditions_text: 100-µm-thick sample; 21 percent O2 level
statement: For 100-µm-thick PMMA, average normal-gravity flame spread was 2.0 mm/s, while the highest microgravity spread rate was about 2.2 mm/s; the report says the microgravity rate was about the same as downward spread.
safety_implication: The similar rates suggest downward spread tests may provide useful context for PMMA spread in microgravity at this oxygen level, but do not establish equivalence across other conditions.
source_quote: The average spread rate over the 100-µm-thick sample in the normal-gravity experiments is found to be 2.0 mm/s (see Figure 2.19(b)). Although the instantaneous spread rate fluctuates slightly, the average spread rate and the flame shape remain relatively steady throughout the experiment. In a microgravity environment, the opposed flow is much lower with experiments conducted mostly at very mild opposed-flow velocities. For the same fuel thickness, the highest spread rate obtained is about 2.2 mm/s

conditions_text: At very high flow velocity, kinetically driven blowoff extinction was observed and at very low velocity (at about 1 cm/s) radiative extinction was observed.
statement: For PMMA flame spread in microgravity, high opposing-flow velocity caused kinetically driven blowoff extinction, while very low velocity at about 1 cm/s caused radiative extinction.
safety_implication: PMMA can extinguish through different mechanisms at opposing-flow extremes, so ventilation changes may affect flame persistence as well as spread.
source_quote: At very high flow velocity, kinetically driven blowoff extinction was observed and at very low velocity (at about 1 cm/s) radiative extinction was observed.

conditions_text: downward spread over PMMA in the thick limit; 10-cm-wide sample
statement: For downward flame spread over thick PMMA in the thick limit, the selected average spread rate was 0.044 mm/s; the reported 10-cm-wide sample value was 0.042 mm/s.
source_quote: Although for thicker fuels, the spread rate is slightly width dependent, a value of 0.042 mm/s for a 10-cm-wide sample (Ref. 23) as opposed to 0.044 mm/s for the 2-cm-wide sample, an average value of 0.044 mm/s is selected as the average spread rate for downward spread over PMMA in the thick limit.

conditions_text: downward flame spread in ambient air
statement: The calculated transition thickness between thermally thin and thick fuels for downward PMMA flame spread in ambient air was 5.19 mm.
safety_implication: Fuel thickness can change which spread-rate regime applies, so flammability assessments of PMMA should account for thickness rather than extrapolate thin-sheet behavior to thicker parts.
source_quote: The transition thickness (2τtransition) can be calculated from this expression as 5.19 mm for downward flame spread in ambient air.

conditions_text: in the absence of external radiant heating
quantity: minimum O2 concentration for flame spread
statement: Black PMMA rods spread flame at oxygen concentrations as low as 17.5 percent in microgravity, while flame spread was not observed below 19 percent in normal gravity; the authors attributed the difference probably to lower opposed-flow velocity in the microgravity tests.
safety_implication: Normal-gravity flammability tests may not establish a conservative oxygen threshold for flame spread in microgravity.
equipment_implication: Account for microgravity flame spread when using normal-gravity flammability test results to set spacecraft material limits.
source_quote: The most important result of the comparison is that of the minimum O2 concentration for flame spread in normal and microgravity. While in microgravity, flame spread was observed at O2 concentrations as low as 17.5 percent, in normal gravity, flame spread was not observed below 19 percent.

statement: Decreasing the diameter of PMMA rods increased flame spread rate in both normal gravity and microgravity, and flame spread was appreciably faster in microgravity than in normal gravity for cylindrical rods.
source_quote: Decreasing the rod diameter increases the flame spread rate in both 1g and microgravity environments, as shown in Figure 4.3. It is also apparent that flame spread in microgravity is appreciably faster than in 1g for cylindrical rods of PMMA.

conditions_text: classic limiting O2 index test; a small sample is burned like a candle flame in a 4-cm/s oxidizer flow velocity
statement: The distinction between flame spread and regression affects interpretation of the limiting O2 index test: near the extinction limit in normal gravity, small flames sit at the top of the sample instead of spreading down it.
safety_implication: A limiting oxygen index result based on top-burning behavior may not represent a material's ability to sustain flame spread along its surface.
equipment_implication: Interpret limiting O2 index results with the distinction between top burning and surface flame spread in mind.
source_quote: The distinction between flame spread and regression is important when one considers the classic limiting O2 index test (Ref. 9), where a small sample is burned like a candle flame in a 4-cm/s oxidizer flow velocity, and the O2 concentration is reduced until the flame extinguishes. The small flames in 1g sit at the top of the sample instead of spreading down the sample near the extinction limit.

conditions_text: concurrent rod geometry; premixed flame oscillations persisted longer in microgravity than in normal gravity
statement: For concurrent PMMA rods, hot material could continue producing fuel vapors after extinction, and the authors recommend maintaining spacecraft fire suppression until the material cools and stops emitting vapors.
safety_implication: Stopping suppression immediately after visible extinction may leave hot material capable of supplying fuel for renewed burning.
equipment_implication: Maintain suppression until the burning material has cooled and stopped emitting vapors.
source_quote: After extinction, the hot material can continue to produce fuel for some time until it cools. Premixed flame oscillations along the rod have been observed for the concurrent rod geometry that persist much longer in microgravity than in normal gravity due to the lower rate of convective cooling of the rod. This suggests that spacecraft fire suppression efforts should be maintained until the burning material has cooled and stopped emitting vapors.

conditions_text: Spread rates decrease as thickness increases, and also decrease as forced-flow velocity decreases (Ref. 10).
statement: For flat PMMA slabs in microgravity, flame spread rate decreased as sample thickness and forced-flow velocity decreased.
source_quote: Spread rates decrease as thickness increases, and also decrease as forced-flow velocity decreases (Ref. 10).

conditions_text: one-sided samples; thickness increased
quantity: extinction oxygen concentration and forced-flow velocity
statement: For one-sided PMMA slabs in microgravity, increasing thickness was associated with a lower oxygen concentration for extinction and a higher forced-flow velocity for extinction.
safety_implication: Material screening should account for thickness because a thicker one-sided slab may remain burning at a higher forced-flow velocity even as its extinction oxygen concentration decreases.
source_quote: For the one-sided samples, there was a clear trend that as thickness increased, the O2 concentration for extinction decreased but the forced-flow velocity for extinction increased.

conditions_text: two-sided samples that spread across the surface compared with one-sided samples
statement: For PMMA slabs that spread across the surface on both sides, extinction velocities were significantly lower than for one-sided samples, indicating greater heat loss to the substrate for one-sided flames.
safety_implication: Flammability assessments of mounted materials should account for substrate heat loss, since it can change the flow conditions at which burning is sustained.
source_quote: For the two-sided samples that spread across the surface, there was not a clear trend with thickness, but the extinction velocities were significantly lower than for the one-sided samples, indicating that heat loss to the substrate for the one-sided flame was significantly greater than the two-sided flame without a substrate.

conditions_text: 1.2-cm-wide versus 2.2-cm-wide regressing samples
statement: For the regressing PMMA samples, 1.2-cm-wide samples extinguished at approximately 1 percent higher O2 than 2.2-cm-wide samples.
source_quote: There was no clear dependence on thickness for the extinction limits for both the 1- and 2.2-cm-wide regressing samples, but the 1.2-cm-wide samples did extinguish approximately 1 percent O2 higher than the 2.2-cm-wide samples, most likely due to increased relative heat losses to the sample holder.

conditions_text: two-sided burns; thin fuels (1-mm-thick)
statement: In the BASS-II two-sided PMMA experiments, higher flow velocity or a thinner sample corresponded to a higher flame spread rate; for 1-mm-thick samples, 2-cm-wide samples spread faster than 1-cm-wide samples.
safety_implication: Width as well as thickness should be represented in material flammability tests, since sample geometry affected measured spread behavior.
source_quote: As you see, the graph illustrates that the higher the flow velocity, or the thinner the sample, the higher the spread rate is. The triangles represent the two model data points, which show a much higher spread rate than experiments (Refs. 9 and 10). On further observation, we can see that the plot exhibits a clear width effect.

conditions_text: one-sided samples compared with two-sided samples
quantity: flame spread rate and opposed-flow rate required to sustain burning
statement: In BASS-II microgravity tests, one-sided PMMA samples burned more slowly than two-sided samples and required a higher opposed-flow rate to keep burning.
safety_implication: Test configurations that expose fuel on both sides may be more conservative for sustaining flame spread than one-sided mounted samples.
source_quote: As shown in Figure 5.9, the one-sided samples burned more slowly than the two-sided samples, and also needed a higher opposed-flow rate to keep burning.

conditions_text: For thin fuels
statement: For thin fuels in the BASS experiments, sample width affects flame spread rate.
source_quote: The two-sided summary graphs show that for thin fuels, sample width affects the spread rate.

conditions_text: two-sided burns compared to one-sided burns
statement: In the BASS experiments, flames spread faster during two-sided burns than during one-sided burns.
source_quote: In general, the flames spread faster for two-sided burns compared to one-sided burns.

conditions_text: different thicknesses that we have tested
statement: In the BASS experiments, increasing solid fuel thickness increased the time for flame spread and reduced the spread rate.
source_quote: The greater the thickness of the fuel, the greater is the time taken for the flame to spread and so the lower is the spread rate.

statement: The model used for the BASS experiments predicted much higher spread rates than the experiments measured.
source_quote: The model currently predicts much higher spread rates than those obtained in the experiment.

conditions_text: ambient O2 concentration in the Microgravity Science Glovebox was varied from 13.6 to 22.2 percent; higher O2 concentrations and as the minimum O2 concentration is approached
statement: In ISS microgravity tests of clear and black PMMA rods, flames were globally stoichiometric at higher oxygen concentrations and became more globally fuel rich near the minimum oxygen concentration because excess pyrolyzate leaked from the open flame tail.
source_quote: O2, CO2, and CO gas sensors provided initial and final readings for each test and indicate that the flames are globally stoichiometric at higher O2 concentrations, but become more globally fuel rich as the minimum O2 concentration is approached due to excess pyrolyzate leakage out of the open tail of the hemispherical flames.

conditions_text: at very low forced flows; quenching and blowoff extinction
statement: For PMMA rods in microgravity, quenching extinction occurred at very low forced flows as the flame shrank to an oscillating hemispherical blue flame; blowoff began when a hole formed in the flame sheet at the stagnation region.
source_quote: Quenching extinction occurs at very low forced flows, where the flame shrinks to a hemispherical blue flame and oscillates with increasing amplitude just before going out. Blowoff extinction is initiated by the formation of a hole in the flame sheet in the stagnation region of the flame.

conditions_text: surface energy balance model; along the flammability boundary
statement: For PMMA rods in microgravity, the surface-energy-balance model's calculated rod regression rates agreed favorably with experimental measurements.
source_quote: The rod regression rates calculated from this model compare favorably with the experimental measurements.

conditions_text: along the blowoff branch; in the quenching region
statement: For PMMA rods along the blowoff branch of the microgravity flammability boundary, heat losses were negligible, while surface radiative loss dominated in the quenching region.
source_quote: The surface energy balance reveals that along the blowoff branch, heat losses are negligible whereas in the quenching region, surface radiative loss dominates.

conditions_text: At the bottom of the flammability map
statement: For PMMA rods at the bottom of the microgravity flammability map, the transition from blowoff to quenching occurred when convective flows became comparable in magnitude to diffusive flows, shifting the critical Damköhler number limitation from residence time to diffusion time.
source_quote: At the bottom of the flammability map, the transition from blowoff to quenching occurs when the convective flows become the same order of magnitude as diffusive flows, shifting the critical Damköhler number from residence time limitations to diffusive time limitations.

conditions_text: At low flows
statement: Prior microgravity tests of PMMA, POM, and HDPE rods reported that flames survived at airflow below 1 cm/s.
source_quote: Flames survived at airflow less than 1 cm/s.

conditions_text: lowest O2 quenching test; approximately 1-cm/s convective flow
statement: For the 0.476-cm-radius rod in the lowest-O2 quenching test, the radiometer detected flame oscillations at approximately 1.1 Hz before the flame extinguished.
source_quote: The radiometer signal oscillates at approximately 1.1 Hz as shown in the inset to Figure 6.6, and drops to a value of 1.05 over a period of a few seconds followed by a large oscillation.

conditions_text: lowest O2 quenching test; measurements just before each flow change
quantity: relationship between flame length and clear bubble layer length
statement: For the 0.476-cm-radius rod in the lowest-O2 quenching test, flame length minus standoff distance matched the clear bubble layer length just before flow changes, indicating that flame heat flux formed the bubble layer.
source_quote: The flame length minus the standoff distance matches the clear bubble layer length just before each flow change, as shown in Figure 6.5, indicating that the bubble layer formation is due to heat flux from the flame, as shown in the flame image inset in Figure 6.5 (at 1,100 s).

conditions_text: opposed-flow flame spread; at any flow
quantity: minimum oxygen concentration for observed flame spread
statement: For opposed-flow flame spread over rods in BASS-II, spread was not observed below 16.4 percent O2 at any flow.
safety_implication: Materials and operating conditions should be assessed for fire spread risk at oxygen concentrations above this observed no-spread range.
source_quote: This is consistent with tests for opposed-flow flame spread over rods that were also done as part of BASS–II (Ref. 14), where opposed-flow flame spread was not observed below 16.4 percent O2 at any flow.

conditions_text: for a given a; 3D cylindrical geometry
statement: For the 3D cylindrical geometry, the two-zone model predicted higher burning rates than the 1D solution at a given stretch rate because it has more surface area for heat transfer and fuel vaporization.
safety_implication: Using a 1D model alone could underestimate burning rates for fuels with cylindrical geometry.
source_quote: The burning rates for the two-zone model are significantly higher than the 1D solution for a given a due to the increased surface area for heat flux and fuel vaporization in the 3D cylindrical geometry.

conditions_text: flow and O2 varied during each test
statement: The two-zone model's predicted average rod regression rates were of the correct magnitude compared with measured average regression rates, although the measured values had significant scatter.
source_quote: There is significant scatter in the measured average regression rates since the flow and O2 varied during each test, but the values are of the correct magnitude compared to the predicted 3D rod regression rates.

conditions_text: Along the flammability boundary; at unity a
statement: Along the flammability boundary at unity stretch rate, the minimum flame heat flux to the surface was 1.57 W/cm2, within the range of literature values for the critical heat flux for PMMA ignition.
source_quote: The minimum heat flux at unity a is 1 W/Ah = 1.57 W/cm2, which is in the range of literature values for the critical heat flux for ignition of PMMA (Ref. 31).

conditions_text: Along the quenching branch
statement: Along the modeled PMMA flammability boundary's quenching branch, fuel vaporization drops sharply as flame-to-surface heat flux falls and heat losses become a significant fraction of that flux.
source_quote: Along the quenching branch, fuel vaporization drops precipitously as the total heat flux to the surface drops and the losses become a significant fraction of the total heat flux to the surface.

conditions_text: during a high-flow blowoff attempt with a flat polymethylmethacrylate sample
statement: During a high-flow blowoff attempt, a flat polymethylmethacrylate sample briefly ejected flame through the open sides of its holder toward the window before extinguishing.
safety_implication: Blowoff can briefly direct flame beyond the sample holder, so nearby surfaces and windows may need protection from flame and soot during suppression.
source_quote: During operations on GMT 205, during a high-flow blowoff attempt with a flat polymethylmethacrylate sample, some flame briefly vapor-jetted out from the open sides of the sample holder toward the window before the flame was extinguished.

conditions_text: At 30 cm/s
statement: For a modeled worst-case thick PMMA slab at 30 cm/s flow, the predicted peak regression rate is 3.13 mm/min.
source_quote: At 30 cm/s, peak regression rate is estimated to be 3.13 mm/min.

conditions_text: The sample is 8.5 cm long, so at 3.05 mm/min
quantity: time for flame base to regress the sample length
statement: The analysis estimates that an 8.5 cm PMMA slab sample would take approximately 28 minutes for the flame base to regress its full length at 3.05 mm/min.
source_quote: The sample is 8.5 cm long, so at 3.05 mm/min, it will take ~28 min for the flame base to regress the entire length of the sample.

quantity: time for flame to grow to steady-state size
statement: The analysis estimates that a PMMA slab flame will grow to steady-state size in approximately 2.5 minutes.
source_quote: To estimate the growth rate, we use an expected power law growth rate (Ref. 3) and estimate the flame will grow to a steady-state size in approximately 2.5 min, as shown in Figure D.3.

conditions_text: thin fabric fuel in concurrent flow; quenching flow velocities were found to be between 1 and 5 cm/s with higher velocity at lower O2 percentage
statement: For SIBAL fabric in concurrent flow in microgravity, quenching flow velocities were between 1 and 5 cm/s, with higher quenching velocities at lower O2 percentages.
safety_implication: Ventilation and oxygen conditions should be considered together when assessing whether a SIBAL-like fabric flame can persist or be quenched in microgravity.
equipment_implication: The measured quenching range can inform low-flow suppression assessments, but does not establish a universal shutdown threshold.
source_quote: Quenching flow velocities were found to be between 1 and 5 cm/s with higher velocity at lower O2 percentage. This trend of the quenching boundary supports the prediction by earlier theoretical models (Refs. 1 and 8).

conditions_text: concurrent flow in microgravity; 1.2-cm-wide sample compared with 2.2-cm-wide sample
statement: The 1.2-cm-wide SIBAL fabric sample had a smaller flammable domain than the 2.2-cm-wide sample in concurrent-flow microgravity tests; its quenching limit was not resolved.
safety_implication: The unresolved limit means these tests do not establish a reliable quenching threshold for the narrower sample.
source_quote: But it can be seen that the narrow sample has a smaller flammable domain, as expected.

conditions_text: 2.2-cm-wide sample in 18.7 percent O2; ignited at 10-cm/s flow; flow reduced to 2.2 cm/s
quantity: flame dimensions and heat-loss behavior during quenching
statement: In the typical SIBAL fabric quenching sequence, reducing flow caused flame length and width to decrease; the shrinking flame lost heat through radiation and, when sufficiently small, conduction before extinction.
equipment_implication: Reducing flow was the means used to approach extinction in this test.
source_quote: As the flow speed was reduced, both flame length and flame width dropped accordingly with flow. After 25 s, flow velocity was reduced to 2.2 cm/s and held there for the remainder of the test. As shown in Figure 7.5, both the flame length and flame width continued to decrease approaching a circular-shaped blue flame seen from the top.

conditions_text: Worst-case assumptions; maximum burn time of 30.5 min.
statement: Under the assumed 30.5-minute worst-case burn, the BASS-II exhaust heat sink was estimated to reach 434 °C, below the lowest-melting hardware material's 660 °C melting point; the entire experiment assembly was estimated to reach 62 °C, and hardware damage was not expected.
safety_implication: The analysis indicates the largest expected BASS-II sample flames should not damage the experiment hardware under the stated assumptions.
equipment_implication: The exhaust heat sink and experiment assembly were estimated to remain below the lowest hardware melting temperature.
source_quote: The maximum temperature if all of the combustion energy is only deposited in this heat sink under these worst-case assumptions, is 434 °C, which is below the melting point of the lowest melting material (aluminum at 660 °C) so this absolute worst-case maximum temperature will not cause damage to the hardware.

conditions_text: One-sided PMMA slab burned at a slow flow; 1-cm-wide sample.
statement: A one-sided PMMA slab burned at slow flow had a reported spread rate of 0.037 mm/s, with its flame reaching a steady size of about 15 mm in about 3 min.
source_quote: In Figure D.6, a one-sided PMMA slab was burned at a slow flow. The 1-cm-wide sample took 7.5 min for the total test time, with the ignition taking over 1 min. Flame reached steady size in about 3 min and was only 15 mm long. The spread rate was 0.037 mm/s (0.0037 cm/s or 2.2 mm/min).

conditions_text: 1-cm PMMA sphere; consumed in four tests at various high- and low-flow speeds; rate calculated from total burn time and sphere surface area.
statement: A 1-cm PMMA sphere consumed over four tests had a reported average burning rate of 1.9 mg/s, corresponding to an estimated surface regression rate of 0.005 mm/s.
source_quote: Sample 19 (1-cm PMMA sphere) was completely consumed in four tests (various high- and low-flow speeds) with the burn durations in Table D.2. The total burn time was 5 min and 25 s (325 s). The average burning rate was 617.5/325 = 1.9 mg/s.
